---
title: "ATAC-seq analysis of liver chromatin accessibility
 Focus on gene regulation and disease progression"
subtitle: "BNFO 420 Capstone"
---

## One-paragraph summary
Cardiometabolic diseases such as diabetes, obesity, and NAFLD are increasing worldwide, and understanding how gene regulation in the liver contributes to these conditions is an important research question. In this project, we used a human liver single-nucleus ATAC-seq dataset containing approximately 68,000 nuclei and over 300,000 accessible chromatin regions across multiple liver samples. We grouped the samples into three steatosis severity categories—NA/None, Mild/Moderate, and Severe—to analyze how chromatin accessibility changes with disease progression. Our approach involved annotating ATAC-seq peaks to genes using tools like ChIPseeker and comparing chromatin accessibility between cardiometabolic genes and control genes, as well as across these steatosis groups. We also applied statistical tests such as Fisher’s Exact Test and ANOVA to determine significance. To present our findings, we generated figures including bar plots, heatmaps, and boxplots to visualize enrichment, genomic location, and disease-related changes in accessibility.

## Abstract

Cardiometabolic diseases, including diabetes, obesity, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), are increasing globally and represent a major public health challenge. The liver plays a central role in metabolic regulation, and disruptions in gene expression within liver cells are closely linked to disease development and progression. Chromatin accessibility is a key regulator of gene expression, as open chromatin regions allow transcription factors and regulatory proteins to bind DNA. ATAC-seq (Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin using sequencing) provides a genome-wide method for identifying these accessible regions, offering insight into gene regulatory mechanisms that may contribute to disease.

In this study, we analyzed a human liver single-nucleus ATAC-seq dataset consisting of approximately 68,000 nuclei and over 300,000 accessible chromatin regions across 39 liver samples. To investigate the relationship between chromatin accessibility and disease progression, samples were grouped into three steatosis severity categories: NA/None, Mild/Moderate, and Severe. Our analysis first evaluated whether cardiometabolic genes are more frequently associated with ATAC-seq peaks compared to control genes. We then examined the genomic distribution of these peaks to determine whether accessible regions are concentrated in regulatory elements such as promoters and introns. Finally, we assessed how chromatin accessibility varies across steatosis severity groups to understand its role in disease progression.

Our results demonstrate that cardiometabolic genes are significantly enriched in accessible chromatin regions, supported by Fisher’s Exact Test (p < 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁶), indicating a strong association between gene type and chromatin accessibility. We also found that ATAC-seq peaks are predominantly located in promoters and introns, highlighting the importance of regulatory DNA in controlling gene expression. Furthermore, analysis across steatosis groups revealed statistically significant differences in chromatin accessibility (ANOVA F = 9.87, p < 0.001), suggesting that chromatin structure changes as disease severity increases.

Overall, these findings suggest that chromatin accessibility plays a critical role in regulating cardiometabolic genes in the liver and may contribute to disease progression. This study provides insight into the epigenetic mechanisms underlying liver disease and highlights the potential for targeting regulatory regions in future therapeutic strategies.
